notes.purpose: Problem, solution, proof and the ask in one view.
notes.script: Problem: the median loan funds in 2.85 days, but a quarter wait more than 15.95 days, and same-day funding fell from 46.0 to 30.3 percent. Solution: loan details predict which loans will be slow, so Kiva can send lender-side support there first: a boosted tree on loan structure catches the slowest fifth 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance. Proof: rewriting stories is not the lever, because five framings stay within five percent of funding time. Our ask: pilot the flag with lender-side support, and test one truthful prompt before giving writing advice. For whom and when is still open: no reliable difference so far, with subgroup results pending.

slides.decision: Our ask to Kiva: pilot a slow-funding flag with lender-side support, and test one truthful prompt.
slides.pending: For whom and when: no period, loan size, gender or region shows a large framing effect; a few rare-word patterns are hypotheses to test.

slides.title: Borrowers usually have the money before lenders fund the loan

takeaways.heading: We study the lender-side step
takeaways.text: Our outcome runs from **listing to full funding**, median 2.85 days.

takeaways.heading: Borrowers usually already have the money
takeaways.text: **96.4% of loans** reach the borrower a median **24.2 days** before listing.

takeaways.heading: Speed turns over partner capital
takeaways.text: Only **3.6%** are paid out after listing, so slow funding mainly holds up the partner’s next loans.

takeaways.heading: Unfunded loans are missing
takeaways.text: Only loans that **eventually funded** are in the data; expired listings are not.

notes.purpose: How a Kiva loan works, and which step we measure.
notes.script: Five stages and four actors. The field partner usually pays the borrower first; Kiva then reviews and lists the loan; lenders fund it; Kiva passes the funds to the partner; and the borrower repays the partner, which repays lenders. For 96.4 percent of loans the borrower already had the money, a median 24.2 days before listing. So the time we measure, from listing to full funding, median 2.85 days, is a lender-side delay: it decides how fast the partner's capital is replenished. Only loans that eventually funded are in the data, so expired listings are missing.

notes.purpose: Define the problem in lender-time terms.
notes.script: Two views of the wait. The yearly chart: same-day funding fell from 42.5 percent in 2019 to 32.3 percent in 2020, a fall of 10.2 points in one year, and stayed near 28 to 30 percent. At the same time the share of loans waiting more than two weeks rose from 19.2 to 35.8 percent; in 2021 that was 55,408 loans. The median wait rose from 1.72 days in 2019 to 4.57 days in 2020 and stayed between 4.49 and 5.35 days through 2024. 2025 may be incomplete, because loans still unfunded at extraction are missing. The strip shows all years together: the median loan is funded in 2.85 days and a quarter within 0.39 days, but a quarter wait more than 15.95 days. That long, predictable tail is why an early-warning flag matters.

notes.purpose: Where the loans and the delays are.
notes.script: Where the loans sit, and where they wait. Ten of 48 countries hold 81 percent of loans, and Asia and Africa 92.8 percent. Speed varies widely: same-day funding runs from 15 percent in Pakistan to 67 percent in Madagascar, and the median wait from 1.13 days in the Philippines to 14.0 days in Tajikistan. In all, 393,847 loans, 27.1 percent, waited more than two weeks, and three countries, Kenya, the Philippines and Tajikistan, hold 56.1 percent of them. Long waits are not a small-country problem: 36.4 percent of Kenya's loans and half of Tajikistan's wait over two weeks. That is why the early warning has to be validated country by country: its precision ranges from 0.18 to 0.90 across the largest countries.

notes.purpose: Show what we measure in each loan.
notes.script: This is an illustrative composite listing, not a real borrower, built from the dataset medians: a US$325 loan over 12 months in agriculture. Most of the listing is fixed. The description is the part a field partner writes, and we score it on eight framing rates per 100 words, family, business, basic needs, agency, gratitude, urgency, first person and third person, plus sentiment and text form. We remove HTML, measure form, count word lists per 100 words and score tone with VADER; the forecasts also use TF-IDF word patterns. The word lists are theory-guided and not yet validated, which is the first gate before any writing advice. Each card shows a plain definition, one example word from its word list and how many descriptions use it at least once. Third-person wording mostly reflects who writes the description, so we treat it as context rather than a lever. The next slides test whether these measures move funding time.

slides.title: Slow funding is a lender-side delay that loan details predict, not wording
slides.subtitle: Three findings across the outcome audit, the early-warning check and the equivalence test, each leading to a step of the solution

cards.heading: The wait is on the lender side
cards.text: of loans reach the borrower before listing

cards.heading: Loan details predict who waits
cards.text: better than chance at flagging the slowest fifth

cards.heading: Wording makes little difference
cards.text: five framings stay within this share of funding time

notes.purpose: Bridge from the problem to the evidence and the solution.
notes.script: Three findings point the same way, and each leads to a step of the solution. First, the wait is on the lender side: 96.4 percent of loans reach the borrower before listing, a median 24.2 days earlier, so the lever is helping slow loans find lenders. Second, loan details predict who waits: a boosted tree on structure flags the slowest fifth 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance. Third, wording makes little difference: five framings stay within five percent of funding time, and text adds little to the flag. That holds across every period, loan size, gender and region we checked, while a few rare-word patterns remain hypotheses to test. So the lever is helping slow loans find lenders, not rewriting their stories. The next slides show the evidence behind each insight.

notes.purpose: Explain how the evidence fits together.
notes.script: All four analyses use the same loans, and each feeds a part of the solution. The explanatory models ask which features are linked to speed, using regressions of funding time and same-day funding with errors clustered by country; because these are associations, they feed the Test step. The robustness checks rerun them with more text measures and a programme proxy, and the equivalence test asks which links are small enough to bound. Together they feed Prioritise: do not chase framing tweaks. The forecast benchmark trains on earlier years and tests each year with and without text; with the early-warning check it feeds Predict. Its numbers are not comparable with the others. Four add-on checks strengthen this: a wild cluster bootstrap and subgroup refits test whether the small associations hold, the gain by feature group shows where the forecast gain comes from, and the early-warning check tests whether a forecast can flag slow loans. The strip shows the years: the explanatory work uses all loans, the holdout tests on 2024 and 2025, and the benchmark retrains five times, each only on loans completed before the test year. None of these is a causal claim.

notes.purpose: Show why we distrust headline significance.
notes.script: With 1.45 million rows almost everything looks significant, because standard HC3 errors treat every loan as independent. When we let errors correlate within each of 48 countries, 64 of the 120 significant terms fell away. [Point: Few countries dominate] The reason is concentration: ten countries hold 81 percent of loans and behave very differently, and regional family-framing patterns rest on two countries each, so they support no regional writing rules; the appendix shows the check. [Point: Text terms are hit hardest] Most of the terms lost are text terms. [Point: Few text terms survive] Only sentiment and some family interactions remain, and the next slide tests the framing terms harder. [Point: Urgency no longer passes] Urgency is the clearest case. For the solution, this means three things: report country-clustered uncertainty rather than only loan-level errors, validate the slow-funding flag country by country before using it, and give no country or regional writing rules from two-country regions. Losing significance is weak evidence, not evidence of no effect; the next two slides ask what survives programme controls and how small the remaining links are.

notes.purpose: Show that one tiny framing link passes the strictest test in one model only.
notes.script: We tested nine framing measures on two outcomes in two models, so 36 tests. Five pass the usual country-clustered test. With 48 countries that test can be too generous, so we re-ran every term with a wild cluster bootstrap, 9,999 draws with Webb weights: four pass. After adjusting for testing nine measures, one passes: third person for funding time in the expanded model, minus 0.9 percent per extra mention, bootstrap p 0.0009 and adjusted p 0.008. With programme controls it does not pass: p 0.128 and adjusted p 0.426. The lowest adjusted p among the others is 0.156. [Point: The one that passes is tiny] In real units, one extra third-person mention per 100 words goes with about 45 to 50 minutes shorter funding time on a typical 2.85-day loan, and one extra business mention with 0.26 to 0.36 points lower same-day funding. These are associations, not effects of an edit. [Point: Loan details are on another scale] On one scale, in the programme-adjusted model, a doubled loan amount, from the 325 dollar median and within its size band, goes with 44.6 percent more on one plus days, a further month of term 8.6 percent, and male rather than female borrowers 61 percent; the framings stay within about 1.5 percent per extra mention. These are associations among completed loans, not levers, and the scale is change in one plus days, not days. That is why Predict starts with loan details. This loan-detail comparison is exploratory and has had one independent code review. [Point: Pronouns may reflect the writer] Third person appears in 97.3 percent of loans and business in 85 percent, so neither is an obvious writing lever. Adding programme controls moves third person only 10 percent towards zero and business 28 percent. Descriptions are usually written by partner staff, so the third-person link may say more about who writes than about the borrower. The next slide asks how small the remaining links really are. One related association on loan content: the sanitation and hygiene sector is modestly faster than the average loan, but the toilets and sanitation activity is not distinguishable from farming once country, time and programme are controlled; the detail is on A4.

notes.purpose: Separate 'small' from 'unknown'.
notes.script: Answer first: five of the nine framings have small links to funding time; urgency and first person remain unknown. How to read the chart: each dot is the estimated change in funding time per extra mention per 100 words, or per half a point of sentiment score, and its line is the 90 percent range. Left of the centre line means faster funding, right means slower. The darker yellow area is within plus or minus five percent of funding time, which we treat as too small to matter; the lighter area runs from five to ten percent. A line that sits wholly inside the darker area means the link is small. [Point: Five framings have small links] Family, business, basic needs, agency and third person sit inside it in both model versions: the expanded model shown here and the programme-adjusted model. Gratitude and sentiment are small only in the programme-adjusted model. [Point: Small means under five hours] Five percent sounds abstract: on a typical loan, which takes 2.85 days to fund, it is about four and a half to four point seven hours. [Point: Urgency is too rare to judge] Urgency and first person appear in under two percent of descriptions, as the right-hand bars show, so their ranges stay wide, reaching six to fourteen percent across the two models. That is not evidence of an effect, or of none. [Point: The verdicts hold under stricter tests] Technically, the band is plus or minus 0.05 on log of one plus days, tested with two one-sided tests, BH-adjusted across nine terms, using a t reference with 47 degrees of freedom. With a stricter t(4) reference all five verdicts hold, and family, agency and third person stay small even at plus or minus two percent. We set the band after seeing the estimates, so this is exploratory. A wild cluster bootstrap across 48 countries, with 9,999 draws, confirms the screen: 35 of 36 verdicts are unchanged and 22 of 23 bounded results survive; the one loss is basic needs for same-day funding in the programme-adjusted model.

slides.solution_link: → Why one playbook serves every group

notes.purpose: Answer for whom and when.
notes.script: For whom and when: we refitted the programme-adjusted model separately in ten subgroups: three periods, three loan sizes, female and male borrowers, and Asia and Africa, and applied the same five percent equivalence test. The five framings from the last slide stay small in all ten, and gratitude joins them in this model; sentiment is small in nine. So the small result is not an average hiding a large effect in one group, and no family-framing interaction with period or loan size survives country clustering. [Point: Rare words stay open in most groups] Urgency is small in one subgroup, first person in five. [Point: Two patterns to test, not to act on] Among about 180 unadjusted tests, urgency in Asia and agency by gender stand out; they are hypotheses for the Test step, not findings. [Point: The count depends on the model] For same-day funding the pattern is weaker: business and third person are small in all ten, family and agency in nine. In the expanded model, family, business, agency and third person stay small in all ten. The bounds were set after the estimates, so this is exploratory. So the solution can use one playbook rather than group-specific story advice.

takeaways.heading: A small gain on a simple model
takeaways.text: Text, mainly **TF-IDF word patterns**, lowers a linear model’s error by 0.26–0.39 days, about 7 hours.

takeaways.heading: About half is context
takeaways.text: Shuffled text keeps **42–61%** of the gain; the loan-specific part is 0.10–0.21 days.

takeaways.heading: A stronger tree gains less
takeaways.text: Fixed trees gain up to **about 0.15 days** from text; tuned trees reach **0.16–0.22** in 2021 (A3).

takeaways.heading: It does not show rewriting helps
takeaways.text: Text alone does worse than loan details, and no forecast tests an edit.

notes.purpose: Keep text in proportion: a small, inconsistent forecast gain that does not drive triage.
notes.script: Answer first: text adds a small and inconsistent forecast gain. [Point: A small gain on a simple model] Added to loan details in a simple linear model, text lowered error by 0.26 to 0.39 days, about seven hours at the median. [Point: About half is context] To see how much is the loan's own words, we shuffled the text among loans in the same country, sector and month. The shuffled text keeps 42 to 61 percent of the gain, so about half is context, such as place and programme templates. The loan-specific part is 0.10 to 0.21 days. [Point: A stronger tree gains less] A larger boosted tree on loan details alone already beats the benchmark tree in four of five years, and with fixed settings adding text gains up to about 0.15 days, under 0.07 in four of five years, and slightly negative in 2024. An exploratory tuned run gains a little more in its best year: 0.16 days for a tuned boosted tree and 0.22 for tuned XGBoost, both in 2021, still below the linear model's gains, and it is near zero in 2023 and 2024. So much of the linear gain looks like a weak baseline catching up. Same-day Brier scores improve in all five years, but by tiny amounts. [Point: It does not show rewriting helps] On its own, text forecasts worse than loan details by 0.146 to 1.032 days, and adding it barely changes the slow-funding flag, so the flag is built on loan details. None of this tests an edit to a description. Text here means description form, word-list counts, VADER sentiment and TF-IDF word patterns; the larger tree uses a compressed version of TF-IDF. The next slide shows how fragile the gain is.

notes.purpose: Keep the gain in proportion: it depends on the model and on which countries are in the sample.
notes.script: Answer first: the linear gain holds across months, but it is fragile across countries and shrinks on a stronger model. One chart: each year has two rows, the linear model and the larger boosted tree. The thick bar is the 95 percent range when we resample calendar months, and the thin line is the range when we resample countries. [Point: Stable across months, linear only] For the linear model, all five thick bars sit right of zero, and the median gain is 0.293 days, about seven hours. [Point: A stronger tree gains little] The violet rows are a larger boosted tree with full text: its ranges exclude zero in three of five years, and by country in only one, and its largest gain with fixed settings is about 0.15 days; tuned trees reach 0.16 to 0.22 in 2021. [Point: Across countries it is fragile] The thin lines resample countries instead: four of the five linear ranges include zero. The scorecard has one dot per test year, 2021 to 2025, filled where the range excludes zero: for the linear model five by month and one by country, for the larger tree three and one, and for the loan-specific part of the gain four and two. [Point: Extreme forecasts explain part of it] Capping forecasts at the longest training wait, 173.4 days, a diagnostic rather than the reported model, leaves only 2025 including zero, so much of the fragility comes from a few extreme forecasts. The loan-specific part of the gain, after removing what shuffled text keeps, clears zero in four of five years by month and two of five by country. Metrics also disagree at the margin: in 2025 text improved error and calibration, but AUC for same-day funding fell from 0.893 to 0.888. Each range uses 1,000 resamples; these are fixed-model resampling ranges, not retraining or causal uncertainty.

slides.title: Our solution: predict slow loans, prioritise support, test before advising
slides.subtitle: A three-step framework for Kiva and partners, built only on what the evidence supports

steps.name: Predict
steps.action: Score each listing’s risk of slow funding when it is posted.
steps.method: A boosted tree on loan structure; text adds little to this score.

steps.name: Prioritise
steps.action: Send lender-side support to flagged loans.
steps.method: Featuring, matching funds, lender alerts and partner follow-up.

steps.name: Test
steps.action: Earn the right to give writing advice.
steps.method: Pass three gates before any advice.

notes.purpose: Turn the evidence into a framework Kiva can act on.
notes.script: Three steps. Predict: at posting time, score each listing’s risk of slow funding. In a retrospective check on the November benchmark, a boosted tree using loan structure flags the slowest fifth of loans 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance; adding text barely changes it. Prioritise: send lender-side support, such as featuring, matching funds, lender alerts and partner follow-up, to the flagged loans, and do not chase framing tweaks, because five framings stay within five percent of funding time; urgency and first person are still unknown. Test: before any writing advice, pass three gates: validate the measures, close the data gaps, and pilot one truthful clarity prompt against a control. Later, a data partnership with listing-time text and unfunded listings would let us answer for whom and when properly. If a gate fails, stop there and report the uncertainty. [Point: Nothing is deployed yet] The flag has only been checked on past loans, and the support levers still need a controlled pilot.

exhibit.lift_label: Lift: top 10% flagged, against the slowest 20% (dashed line: random, 1×)

notes.purpose: Show the flag adds something a simple lookup does not, without overclaiming.
notes.script: This is a concept to pilot, not a product. When a loan is posted, a model scores its risk of slow funding from loan details: amount, term, sector, country and timing. [Point: Better than a simple lookup] A fair comparison is a historical lookup: the typical funding time for the same country, sector and calendar month, taken from training years. Flagging the top ten percent of predicted-slow loans, the boosted tree catches the slowest fifth 2.63 to 4.04 times better than chance, against 1.97 to 2.74 for the lookup, and it is higher in all five years. An exploratory bootstrap puts 95 percent ranges on that gap: above zero in all five years by month blocks, lowest 0.22, and by country blocks, lowest 0.08, both in 2021. Within-country precision margins are also above zero by month blocks, lowest 0.15. 2021 is the thinnest year: for the larger and tuned trees the country-block range includes zero that year. [Point: Clearest within a country] Within a country the gap is widest: median precision is 0.49 to 0.56 for the tree and 0.22 to 0.29 for the lookup, where random is 0.20. So the flag is not simply naming slow countries. [Point: Text adds little to the flag] Adding text barely changes it. [Point: Checked looking back only] The check covers completed loans only and looks back; precision ranges from 0.18 to 0.90 across the ten largest countries; the predicted probabilities drift in 2025, so they need recalibrating before use as thresholds; and a flag says a loan is likely slow, not why. For the boosted tree on funding time, the month-block range for that text change includes zero in four of five years. For reference, the primary 24-hour model ranks same-day funding with ROC AUC 0.8997 on later loans.

slides.title: Send lender-side support to flagged loans, not story edits
slides.subtitle: Proposed levers for Kiva and partners; their effect on speed is to be tested, not yet measured

levers.name: Feature it
levers.text: Show flagged loans to lenders early on the lending page.

levers.name: Match it
levers.text: Offer matching funds where a loan is likely to stall.

levers.name: Alert lenders
levers.text: Notify lenders who follow the loan’s sector or country.

levers.name: Follow up
levers.text: Ask the field partner to check the listing is complete and clear.

dont.heading: Don’t chase framing tweaks
dont.text: The evidence points away from wording, so effort goes to the loan.

slides.note: Scope: the levers are proposals; our data do not measure their effect.

notes.purpose: What to do with a flag.
notes.script: A flag only helps if something happens next. We propose four lender-side levers: feature flagged loans early, offer matching funds where a loan is likely to stall, alert lenders who follow the sector or country, and ask the partner to check the listing is complete. Our data do not measure what these levers do, so each needs a pilot. What we can say is where not to spend effort: framing tweaks, because five framings stay within five percent of funding time, about four and a half hours on a typical loan.

takeaways.text: Each changes **who sees a flagged loan** or what support it gets, not the story.

takeaways.heading: Each has a cost to watch
takeaways.text: Featuring can crowd out other loans; matching uses money; alerts can **tire lenders**.

takeaways.heading: Their effect is unmeasured
takeaways.text: Our data cannot say what these levers do, so **each needs a controlled pilot**.

takeaways.heading: Wording is not the lever
takeaways.text: The evidence so far gives **no reason to rewrite stories** to speed funding.

slides.title: Four limits decide what the solution can claim today
slides.subtitle: What this evidence cannot show, and what to do about it

notes.purpose: Limits, each with an action.
notes.script: Four guardrails. [Point: Claims stay at association level] One: every result is an association; nothing has been tested by editing a description or applying a lever, so each needs a controlled pilot. [Point: Reach stays an open question] Two: only funded loans are in the data, so we cannot say whether a lever helps loans that would otherwise expire. [Point: The flag is validated by country] Three: the flag is uneven across countries, with precision from 0.18 to 0.90 within the ten largest, and its probabilities drift in 2025, so it must be recalibrated and validated by country. [Point: One passing signal is not a rule] Four: for whom and when: framings stay small across periods, loan sizes, genders and regions, regional patterns rest on two countries each, and the one framing link that passes the strictest test does so in one model only, so no writing rule follows. The strip under the rows shows where each limit gets addressed: country validation comes with the flag rollout, the data gap at gate 2, and the causal and writing questions at the gate 3 pilot. Funding time is also a platform measure: 96.4 percent of loans reach the borrower before listing.

notes.purpose: Compare every model in one place and state what each score means.
notes.script: This slide puts every forecaster on one scale. Lower is better. The median and lookup models are simple baselines. A linear model on loan details beats the lookup in every year, and a boosted tree beats the linear model. The larger tree is better in four of five years but worse in 2021. Those settings were fixed in advance, which keeps the text comparison matched. To check that choice, an exploratory run tuned a boosted tree and XGBoost on the year before each test year, 24 settings each, chosen on loan details and reused with text. Tuning did not clearly help: on loan details alone, tuned trees were lowest in 2023, 2024 and 2025, by at most 0.06 days, while fixed settings were lower in 2021 and 2022, by 0.54 and 0.38 days. XGBoost beat the tuned boosted tree in 2 of 5 years. The tuned models forecast days only, so they have no same-day score. The August models are a separate chronological holdout with library defaults, so do not compare those numbers with the benchmark. Across all sixteen forecasters, the lowest error each year is marked in yellow: the tree with programme and text in 2021 and 2025, the larger tree with text in 2022, tuned XGBoost in 2023 and the tuned tree in 2024. Programme text is an unvalidated proxy.

takeaways.text: Moving from a lookup to a model on loan details cuts error in **every year**.

takeaways.heading: Bigger is not always better
takeaways.text: The larger tree beats the benchmark tree in 4 of 5 years, but **not in 2021**.

takeaways.heading: Tuning did not clearly help
takeaways.text: On loan details, tuned trees were lowest in 3 of 5 years, **by at most 0.06 days**.

takeaways.heading: XGBoost is no clear winner

glossary: **MAE**: average miss in days; lower is better.
**R²**: variation explained; below 0 is worse than the mean.
**ROC AUC**: ranks same-day loans; 0.5 is random, 1 is perfect.
**Brier** 0.1156: same-day probability error; lower is better.

notes.script: This uses the full programme-adjusted model rather than the 20,000-loan topic sample. Education, health and manufacturing loans fund much faster than the average loan, while food, retail and clothing fund slower. Toilets and sanitation look very fast in raw means, 0.9 days, and in the sample themes on A5. notes.purpose: Show the themes in full and why their raw speed should not be read as a theme effect.
notes.script: These eight themes come from an exploratory topic model on a 20,000-description sample, so treat them as a sample view. Each loan is assigned its dominant theme. [Point: Two themes look very fast] Sanitary and water themes have raw means of 1.5 and 1.8 days and medians near half a day or less. The other six average 7.3 to 13.5 days. [Point: That speed is mostly context] With loan details, country and time held fixed, against the average theme, sanitary is minus 17.5 percent, range minus 39.4 to plus 12.3, and water is minus 12.6 percent, range minus 42.2 to plus 32.2. Both ranges include zero. Adding activity moves them to plus 4.9 and plus 3.4 percent. So they fund fast, but that speed largely reflects which countries and loan types they are. [Point: Only pig raising holds up] With loan details held fixed, pig raising, Philippines business and general store are slower than average, at plus 8.6, plus 6.1 and plus 17.8 percent. With activity added, only pig raising stays clear, plus 8.5 percent, range plus 2.4 to plus 15.1, and that is before correcting for eight comparisons. [Point: A sample, not a lever] These are associations among completed loans. A loan's theme is not something to change.

exhibit.note_sup: Groups added in order: form, then lexicon and sentiment, then TF-IDF; another order would split the gain differently.
exhibit.chart_title: Adding text lowers linear error in every year
exhibit.chart_guide: MAE in days, linear model; 728,640 records, with and without text.

takeaways.heading: A small linear gain
takeaways.text: Gains of **0.26–0.39 days** on 728,640 evaluation records; about half is context.

takeaways.heading: Forecasting is not persuasion
takeaways.text: Text may encode **purpose, place or programme templates**, not only persuasion.

takeaways.heading: No single country drives it
takeaways.text: Removing any single country **leaves the gain positive** in every year (exploratory check).

takeaways.heading: Word patterns carry most of it
takeaways.text: TF-IDF gives the largest share in **4 of 5 years**; lexicon and sentiment add only **0.003–0.055 days**.

notes.purpose: Present the strongest new result.
notes.script: We trained on earlier years and tested on each of 2021 to 2025, comparing the same model with and without text on the same loans. Text reduced the linear model's error every year; shuffled-text and larger-tree checks in the main deck show about half of that is context and a stronger tree with fixed settings gains up to about 0.15 days, and tuned trees reach 0.16 to 0.22 in 2021. [Point: A small linear gain] [Point: Word patterns carry most of it] Splitting the gain by feature group, added in a fixed order, word patterns from TF-IDF give most of it in four of five years; 2023 is the exception, where description form leads. The lexicon, specificity and sentiment measures, the ones closest to framing, add only 0.003 to 0.055 days. Text alone forecasts worse than structure alone in every year, so text adds to context rather than replacing it.
